commentary.bottom_line: Nineteen sources, mostly voluntary frameworks, professional guidance, and commentary, endorse documented lifecycle gates and recurring reviews of deployed AI, but no supplied study tests whether the practice keeps AI under oversight as performance or context changes. The recommendation currently rests on expert consensus rather than measured effect.

perspectives.view: No study testing the practice and no study documenting the hazard was supplied. The endorsements consist of frameworks, guidance, and commentary, which GRADE treats as expert opinion. Agreement across 19 sources shows consistency of opinion, but it cannot establish that recording owners, evidence, approval status, and review triggers changes outcomes.

The CHAI guide describes checkpoints during silent deployment, pilot, and at regular intervals afterward. The logic is that scheduled review may catch performance degradation before patients are harmed. No supplied study measures how often such reviews detect drift, how quickly they do so, or whether detection prevents harm.

The radiology multi-society statement leaves the definition of sufficient monitoring to each local oversight group, case by case. This suggests that review content and frequency may vary widely between sites. No supplied study reports the staff burden of lifecycle gates or how faithfully organizations carry out scheduled reviews.

The supporting sources are voluntary. CHAI playbooks rate intake and lifecycle documentation as a must, while the NIST generative AI profile and most guidance rate related activities as should. None of the supplied endorsements comes from a binding regulation, so adoption depends on organizational choice.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares organizations or AI tools with and without documented lifecycle gates and recurring reviews. Useful designs would measure time from performance degradation to detection, the share of deployed tools with a named owner and current review, patient-level harm events, and the staff hours and cost per review cycle.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is unknown whether recurring reviews, as practiced, examine performance in these groups or whether safety-net systems have the staff to sustain them.
